title_content.content: Bartonella, Rodents, Fleas and Ticks: a Molecular Field Study on Host-Vector-Pathogen Associations in Saxony, Eastern Germany

paragraph_content.content: Cornelia Silaghi1,2 & Martin Pfeffer3 & Daniel Kiefer1,4 & Matthias Kiefer5 & Anna Obiegala3

Abstract Bartonellae cause zoonotic diseases and are transmitted by arthropods. Rodents are reservoirs for most Bartonella spp. As the knowledge about Bartonella in rodents and their parasitizing ectoparasites is scarce in Germany, this study’s objectives were to investigate Bartonella spp. in small mammals and in their ectoparasites. A total of 79 small mammals (seven species) were captured and their ectoparasites collected at seven sites around Leipzig, Saxony, Germany, in 2010 and 2011. Altogether, 79 spleen samples, 135 fleas (five species) and 365 ticks (three species) were investigated for Bartonella spp. by PCR targeting the ITS 16S–23S rRNA region. In total, 52
ticks were positive for Bartonella spp. Most small mammals were positive for uncultured Bartonella sp.
. Likewise, most fleas were positive for uncultured Bartonella sp.

. This study’s results suggest that rodents and fleas may be reservoirs and vectors, respectively. Zoonotic B. grahamii and B. elizabethae were found in rodents and their fleas. Therefore, humans may contract Bartonella infection by contact to wild rodents. Ticks seem of minor importance in transmitting Bartonella spp. found in fleas and rodents. However, ticks might be vectors of B. chomelii.
Ctenophthalmus nobilis . Bartonella spp. . Ixodes ricinus

Bartonella spp. are facultative intracellular alphaproteobacteria (order Rhizobiales, family Bartonellaceae) and the causative agents of bartonellosis which may result in severe clinical symptoms in humans and domesticated animals worldwide [39]. Bartonellosis, depending on the infecting Bartonella species, may cause chronical (e.g. verruga peruana) and acute (e.g. cat scratch fever) infections displayed by a variety of clinical symptoms [26, 40]. Bartonella quintana, Bartonella bacilliformis and Bartonella henselae are the most common causative agents and are carried by humans and cats (B. henselae) respectively [39]. However, there is an increasing number of clinical reports in humans caused by other bartonellae such as Bartonella elizabethae and Bartonella grahamii which are harboured by rodents [53]. While varying prevalences of bartonellae were found in wild ungulates, carnivores and domesticated animals [9, 12, 19, 32], the highest prevalence and diversity of Bartonella spp. were reported in rodents which are considered to be main reservoirs. in studies from Poland [35, 54], Slovenia [21], Spain [13], France [8] and the UK [49].

Bartonella spp. are mainly transmitted by haematophagous arthropod vectors such as fleas, lice, sandflies and ticks [2, 4, 14, 44]. Other vectors such as the woodlouse hunter spider (Dysdera crocata) have been suggested as vectors as well [27]. Amongst ectoparasites infesting rodents, fleas are expected to be main vectors for Bartonella spp. [3, 52]. Ctenophthalmus nobilis also known as Ctenophthalmus agyrtes, the most common flea species parasitizing rodents in Central Europe, is known to transmit B. grahamii and B. taylorii to Myodes glareolus [5]. In European countries such as Poland [38], Italy [42], the Netherlands [44] and France [15], Bartonella spp. were detected in Ixodes ricinus, the most common tick in Central Europe [41]. However, data on Bartonella species in rodents and their parasitizing ectoparasites, such as C. nobilis and I. ricinus, is lacking in Germany and information about host-vector-pathogen associations of the latter are scarce in Europe. Thus, this study’s objectives were to analyse (1) the occurrence of Bartonella species in rodents, their fleas and ticks and (2) to identify their host-vector-pathogen associations in Germany.

The study site was divided in five animal trapping areas located around the city centre of Leipzig in Saxony which were formerly consecutively named from E to I [45]. Sites E–G are part of the BLeipziger Neuseenland^ (http://www. leipzigerneuseenland.de/), a recultivated former brown coal mining area which is surrounding a lake (Lake Cospuden, 436 ha) and which belongs to the largest recreational area near Leipzig. Site H is a recreational city park called BPark Lößnig-Dölitz^ (http://www. leipzig.de/de/buerger/freizeit/leipzig/parks/park_loessnig/) , near Leipzig which contains several ponds. This park merges into forested areas and is located near a renatured waste disposal mountain. Site I (42 ha) is a game park, located in Leipzig, often frequented by visitors, which belongs to one of the largest riparian forests in Germany (www.leipziger-auwald.de). About 250 game animals are present (http://www.leipzig.de/de/buerger/
freizeit/leipzig/parks/wildpark/wissen/). The study site and trapping areas have been described in detail in previous studies [45].
Small mammals were trapped with Sherman

live animal traps (H. B. Sherman Traps, Inc., Tallahassee, FL, USA) in 2010 and 2011 (official trapping permit: 36.11-36.45.12/4/10- 026-MH, 364.60/2009-102-2). Traps, baited with apple slices, were placed for at least two consecutive nights per month and site and were checked twice a day. Small mammals were captured with at least 20 traps per subdivided area per month in August and October in 2010, from March to June in 2011 (sites E, H, I) and further in November 2011. Collected animals were anaesthetized with

until further examinations in the laboratory. Details about small mammal trapping were published before [30]. All small mammals were morphologically identified [48]. Bycaught small mammal species, found dead in traps or brought by a cat, were additionally verified by the use of a conventional PCR targeting the partial cytochrome
gene (354 bp) as described previously [34, 45]. Necropsy was carried out and spleens from the small mammals were collected.
Ectoparasites were collected from the trapped small mammals with tweezers and stored separately for each small mammal in 1.5-ml-sized tubes at

(Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany) until further examination. The morphological identification of fleas and ticks was performed under a stereomicroscope with standardised taxonomic keys [17, 36, 37, 47]. Fleas and ticks were kept individually in separate 2.0-ml-sized tubes (Eppendorf) for the following DNA extraction.

DNA extraction from collected fleas was carried out for each flea individually with the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) as previously described [46]. Quantity and quality of the extracted DNA were determined with a spectrophotometer (Nano Drop ND-1000, Erlangen, Germany).
A conventional PCR targeting 635 bp of the 16S–23S ITS region was performed for detection of Bartonella spp. as
described [25, 43], followed by UV light analysis on
agarose gel dyed with GelRed (Biotium, Hayward CA, USA).

PCR products were purified with the QIAquick PCR product purification Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and sequenced commercially by Eurofins MWG Operon (Martinsried, Germany). Sequences were analysed with Chromas Lite® (Technelysium Pty Ltd., South Brisbane, Australia) and compared with sequences obtained from GenBank using BLASTn (National Center for Biotechnology Information, Bethesda MD, USA) as previously described [43]. Analysed and aligned sequences were deposited in GenBank under the following Acc. Nos.: KU886369–KU886524.

The complexity of relations between Bartonella spp., flea and rodent species is shown in Fig. 1. In both fleas and in rodents, uncultured Bartonella spp. were most commonly detected. The figures shows clearly that Bartonella spp. detected in most flea and rodent species are very diverse and that there is just a single host-vector-pathogen association between M. glareolus, Me. turbidus and B. grahamii.

In comparison to other mammals, the highest diversity of Bartonella spp. was described in rodents to date. Altogether, 22 rodent-associated Bartonella spp. and subspecies were described [14]. Some of them were initially isolated from infected humans [8]. The prevalences for Bartonella spp. in rodents from other European countries such as Poland, Denmark, England and Sweden ranged between 11 and

A. flavicollis was significantly more often infected with Bartonella spp. than M. glareolus in the present study. This observation was made before and it was not explained by the different ecologic habitats of both of these rodent species but rather by specific hostpathogen interactions. While M. glareolus is able to resolve Bartonella infections within 1–2 months, the duration of resolving the infection is still not definitely known for

A. flavicollis [35]. Moreover, it has been observed that reinfection in M. glareolus is more seldom than in A. flavicollis [35]. The flea abundance might directly influence the prevalence of Bartonella infection in the rodent host. Overall, fleas were found significantly more often on Apodemus spp. than on M. glareolus in this study. This may also explain why Apodemus spp. were more often infected with Bartonella sp. than M. glareolus. Furthermore, M. glareolus, in contrast to other small mammal species such as Peromyscus leucopus, is not able to transmit Bartonella spp. transplacentally [5, 23]. This is why vectors are important for the maintenance of Bartonella in these reservoir hosts. B. grahamii was more abundant in M. glareolus than in Apodemus spp. in our study. Previously, it has been reported that M. glareolus is the main

paragraph_content.content: reservoir for B. grahamii [53]. A former study reported that B. grahamii may be transmitted to the paws of cats by infected rodents which were killed by cats, as contact samples of cat paws were positive [31]. In this way, this pathogenic Bartonella species may be further transmitted by cat scratches to other animals and humans [31].

T. europaea and Ar. terrestris were, though not infested with fleas, positive for Bartonella spp. in our study. It is probable that those small mammals, which were found dead due to being caught by a cat, were not infested with fleas due to the survival strategy of fleas which jump off dead hosts as soon as the hosts’ body temperature is decreasing [18]. The high infestation rate of fleas on small mammals at site BI^ could be due to the high density of captured rodents and may explain why the majority of Bartonella-positive rodents were found there. Fleas vary greatly in their degree of host specificity, from being highly host-specific to host-opportunistic [24]. Most flea species showed a preference for certain rodent species in our study. As Me. turbidus was found predominantly on
. glareolus and C. nobilis and N. fasciatus significantly more often on Apodemus spp., it seems likely that these flea species have a host preference, but no clear host specificity.
In our study, the prevalences for Bartonella spp. were high in most rodent flea species such as C. nobilis

). There are only few studies investigating those flea species for the occurrence of Bartonella spp. However, B. taylorii and B. grahamii are known to be transmitted by C. nobilis to M. glareolus [5]. Bartonella sp. has previously been described in N. fasciatus [33]. The prevalence of Bartonella spp. in fleas seemed to be independent of the Bartonella species and of the prevalence in their rodent hosts as most positive fleas derived either from negative rodents or from rodents which were not positive for the same Bartonella species. This observation has been made before, with the conclusion of a vertical transmission path for Bartonella in fleas [7]. B. grahamii, B. taylorii and B. elizabethae are known to occur in fleas which infest rodents [53]. In our study, these Bartonella spp. as well as several uncultured Bartonella spp. were found in fleas. Though B. elizabethae is known to occur in rodents and fleas, we detected this Bartonella species exclusively in fleas [6].

B. grahamii was more abundant in Me. turbidus fleas compared to other flea species. In accordance with this finding, B. grahamii was mainly found in M. glareolus, the main host of Me. turbidus, suggesting a host-vector-pathogen association for M. glareolus, Me. turbidus and B. grahamii. Apart from this observation, no other significant host-vectorpathogen associations were found.

To date, it is not clear whether ticks are involved in the natural life cycle of Bartonella spp. Their epidemiological importance has been considered secondary [16, 28, 50]. However, previous studies from Italy, France, Portugal and Germany reported prevalences ranging between 1.5 and
in questing I. ricinus ticks respectively in I. ricinus removed from humans [10, 15, 20, 42]. In our study, the prevalence is in the range of the mentioned European studies (

). The Bartonella species detected in ticks in this study were B. chomelii, B. grahamii, B. taylorii and uncultured Bartonella sp. The prevalence in I. ricinus was significantly higher when compared to

. reticulatus. Thus, D. reticulatus appears to be less important in the transmission cycle of Bartonella spp. than I. ricinus. Comparing the results for Bartonella in ticks and fleas, ticks seem to be more dependent on the prevalence and Bartonella sp. detected in their rodent hosts in contrast to fleas. Most positive ticks were collected from positive rodents in our study, and the Bartonella sp. found in ticks were mainly matching the species found in their rodent hosts. These results suggest that ticks, reflecting the infection in their rodent hosts, are of minor importance in the natural life cycle of Bartonella spp. found in rodents and their fleas. However, B. chomelii was exclusively found in ticks but not in fleas and rodent hosts from this study. Formerly, B. chomelii was detected in domesticated ruminants and in their engorged ticks from Spain and Italy [1, 11]. Cattle are suggested to be reservoirs not showing any clinical symptoms [1]. As B. chomelii has never been detected in fleas and rodents thus far, this Bartonella sp. is likely to be transmitted transovarially in tick populations in nature as most positive ticks deriving from rodents were larvae which were naïve before feeding on their rodent hosts.

In conclusion, a high prevalence of different Bartonella species was found in rodents and their fleas with a high diversity and a tendency towards a host-vector-pathogen association for M. glareolus, Me. turbidus and B. grahamii. Zoonotic bartonellae such as B. grahamii and B. elizabethae were found in rodents and their fleas in this study. Therefore, humans and their companion animals are at risk of contracting Bartonella infection by direct or indirect contact to infected blood of wild living rodents. Ticks seem to be of minor importance in the transmission cycle of Bartonella sp. found in fleas and rodents. However, ticks may play an important role as vectors in the transmission of B. chomelii.
